State governments must also accept responsibility for the worsening living conditions of their citizens. With substantial increases in allocations from the Federation Account Allocation Committee (FAAC) and improved internally generated revenue (IGR) in several states, governors have little justification for failing to deliver tangible improvements in public services.
The problem increasingly appears to be one of misplaced priorities, fiscal indiscipline and weak accountability.
The 2026 State of States Report released by BudgIT exposes this contradiction. FAAC allocations to the 35 states more than doubled within a year, rising from approximately N5.4 trillion in 2023 to N11.38 trillion in 2024.
Sadly, these additional resources have not translated into corresponding improvements in the lives of millions of Nigerians struggling with rising food, healthcare, transportation and housing costs, as well as declining purchasing power.
Expenditure patterns highlighted in the report raise serious questions about governors’ priorities. Abia State, for instance, spent N150.54 billion on construction in 2025, compared with N96.29 billion on health, education, agriculture and water supply combined. More disturbing is the poor utilisation of allocations to critical sectors. Of its revised health budget of N74.11 billion, only N26.03 billion was spent, while agriculture received just N1.95 billion out of N18.84 billion.
Although Abia’s 2022 multidimensional poverty rate of 29.8 per cent was considerably below the national average of 63 per cent, approximately 1.12 million residents were still classified as poor. This suggests that significant deprivation persists despite the state’s relatively better poverty profile, making the government’s spending priorities even more difficult to justify.
Roads and other infrastructure are important, but development cannot be measured simply by the number of roads constructed, flyovers commissioned or public buildings erected. Agriculture, healthcare, education and access to clean water are equally important indicators. A government cannot claim success when substantial resources go into construction while essential services remain inadequately funded.
The problem is compounded by the rising cost of governance. In Abia, expenditure on governance nearly doubled from N64.19 billion in 2024 to N126.68 billion in 2025, with overhead costs rising by 197.07 per cent to N70.87 billion. Oyo State recorded an 88.85 per cent increase in operating expenses to N372.68 billion, while Lagos State’s rose by 23.89 per cent to N1.29 trillion.
At a time when citizens are making painful sacrifices to survive, such increases demand explanations. Governors must demonstrate the value citizens receive from the rising cost of running government. Expanding bureaucracies and administrative expenditure should not take precedence over functional hospitals, schools and other essential services.
Poor budget implementation is another concern. An expenditure analysis presented alongside the BudgIT report showed that 34 states approved combined budgets of N35.22 trillion for the first half of 2026 but spent only N8.60 trillion, representing 24.4 per cent. This left N26.62 trillion in approved expenditure unspent at the halfway point.
This points to serious weaknesses in the states’ capacity and commitment to execute their budgets.
The consequences are evident in hospitals without adequate equipment and essential drugs, overcrowded classrooms, out-of-school children, poorly supported farmers and communities without reliable water supply and proper waste disposal facilities. Unimplemented budgetary allocations amount to a denial of essential services to already hard-pressed citizens.
The contradiction between revenue generation and poverty reduction is particularly evident in Enugu and Ogun states.
According to BudgIT, Enugu’s IGR increased by 125.91 per cent, from N180.5 billion in 2024 to N407.76 billion in 2025. This placed it among the country’s leading states in revenue mobilisation and earned it second position in the overall fiscal performance ranking.
Yet, the 2022 National Bureau of Statistics (NBS) Multidimensional Poverty Index puts Enugu’s poverty rate at 63.1 per cent, affecting approximately 2.63 million people, virtually at the national average of 63 per cent. BudgIT also observed that non-tax receipts accounted for 90.79 per cent of the increase in IGR, raising questions about the sustainability of the growth and whether it reflects a corresponding expansion of the productive economy.
Ogun State presents a similar contradiction. Its IGR increased by 29.2 per cent, from N194.93 billion in 2024 to N252.36 billion in 2025. Yet, its multidimensional poverty rate stood at 68.1 per cent, above the national average, with approximately 3.78 million residents classified as poor.
Given its industrial activities, economic advantages and proximity to Lagos, Ogun should be better positioned to expand employment opportunities and reduce deprivation. Governor Dapo Abiodun must demonstrate how the state’s growing revenue base is translating into better healthcare, education and economic opportunities. Similarly, Governor Peter Mbah’s administration in Enugu must show how increased revenue is improving citizens’ welfare rather than merely enhancing fiscal statistics.
Although these state poverty figures are based on 2022 data, more recent national statistics offer little encouragement. A report by the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) and the Oxford Poverty and Human Development Initiative (OPHI) shows that an additional 17.9 million Nigerians fell into multidimensional poverty between 2021 and 2024, the largest increase recorded by any country during the period assessed. The 2026 Global Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI) puts Nigeria’s multidimensional poverty rate at 38.7 per cent in 2024, up from 33 per cent in 2021. The number of affected people consequently increased from 72.2 million to 90.1 million.
These figures reinforce the point that improved fiscal rankings do not automatically translate into better living conditions. What matters is how effectively available resources are deployed to address citizens’ needs. Enugu and Ogun have demonstrated considerable capacity to generate revenue internally, yet their poverty rates remain high. Abia, meanwhile, has a considerably lower poverty rate, but its expenditure priorities raise concerns about its commitment to sustaining human development.
Governors must recognise that poverty reduction requires sustained investment in agriculture, small businesses, public education, primary healthcare, rural roads, electricity and water supply. These are the foundations for expanding economic opportunities, improving productivity and lifting households out of poverty.
Ultimately, state governors must spend less on political vanity and more on the people. The true measure of fiscal performance is not how much money enters government coffers, how large budgets are or how many projects are commissioned, but how effectively public resources are deployed to improve lives and lift citizens out of poverty. This responsibility rests squarely on the shoulders of state governors.
